items.content:
RT @Jhaddix: AI Psychosis is a real thing. 

It happens to smart people. 

It manifests in different ways. 

Some people don’t have the ability to understand AI hallucinations from fact. 

Others do, but they have had success using AI and stop applying critical thinking and review to it. 

For some people it manifests as over investing in an unhealthy relationship with a chatbot. 

For others, it’s the constant pressure to produce with a very capable new tool. Or being able to produce something without the base skills but not understanding that the product is flawed in its design. 

In subtle cases, it’s people *outsourcing* their critical thinking and review skills to AI. 

In other cases it’s blind trust of the capabilities of the technology. 

Sometimes it can be blind trust of the technology vendors who make the models. Like a cult following. 

It’s all very scary. It’s hard to break people out of. And it’s only going to get worse.

items.content:
New MaaS malware using a Polygon blockchain smart contract as both a C2 fallback and a kill switch. If the smart contract returns fewer than 10 bytes, the malware self-terminates.

TELEPUZ is a modular malware spreading via ClickFix social engineering through VIDAR. Lightweight, hand-written C, actively developed since April 2026.

Indirect syscalls patched as trampoline stubs into random legitimate DLLs at runtime. NTDLL unhooking from a fresh mapped copy. AMSI and ETW patched out. DLL notification callbacks stripped. Anti-VM, anti-debug, and CIS country exclusion.

Fallback C2 resolution through four independent channels: Telegram, Steam profile names, DNS records, and Polygon blockchain. WebSocket C2 with TLS.

36 commands. Process hollowing. Token theft. UAC bypass via COM elevation moniker and AppInfo ALPC with DebugObjects. Modular stealer, keylogger, web injector using Chrome DevTools Protocol without ever injecting into the browser. Shellcode injection command still returns "INJECT:TODO" confirming active development.

Full IOCs and YARA rules included.

https://t.co/LDRCQFYZiV

items.content:
RT @vxunderground: I've praised a few malwares for various reasons. However, this particular malware is very interesting.

- Initially masquerading malware, designed to target very specific audience 

- Written in multiple programming languages. However, the first stage is written in an uncommon programming language (Delphi) and compiled using an uncommon compiler (Embarcadero), specifically Delphi GUI TForm from Embarcadero (Vcl?)

- Obfuscated, in a very natural way. The binary at first glance appears semi-legitimate, it hides itself well

- The first stage (stager, or packer) contains multiple layers of decoy data. It makes reverse engineering challenging, not due to difficulty but time exhaustion

- Secondary stage (where I'm currently at) is loaded into memory discretely, it flows naturally with the GUI application. When decompiled, the stager has over 15,000 functions. It makes finding the in-memory loaded secondary stage tricky

- The secondary stage has some form of interprocess communication, it relies on the first stage to load it. If the first stage is not present, it does not work.

- The second stage works (in a currently unknown capacity) to load a third stage payload. However, the secondary stage with the first stage work (in a currently unknown way) to decrypt the third (and potentially final) stage a/k/a the actual payload

- The second stage uses deterministic probability to alert the first stage if the machine executing the first stage is a virtual machine and/or anti malware environment.

- The second stage has multiple integrity checks, it ensures it has not been tampered with to force the binary to pull the third and final stage.

This malware is pretty tricky. It definitely hasn't been written by a noob. This is definitely a very skilled Threat Actor who is using AI to supercharge their code base. Based on my conversations with my colleague, and information he can share, this code base has been rapidly evolving over the past couple of months in a uncharacteristic manner. While this Threat Actor has always shown evolution and improvement, it is now much faster, precise, and flexible.

Overall, based on what I've seen so far, they've put in a lot of work to make this as painful as possible. In order to successfully reverse engineer this binary, it require outside the box thinking and/or building a custom solution to successfully trick the secondary stager to give up the goop (the third stage)... or a custom extractor to pull the third stage statically.

No solution is ideal. This is good malware. If it's not state-sponsored, it's someone who has been doing this a long time and knows ball.

RT @nextronresearch: 📷 We've identified a Linux backdoor under development

Archive Hash 76a360593bf7b068649dcbd8056952a569ebf3a9f7bae480015a7fffc306c5dd  

== Components Identified

PAM Backdoor
7531643f797206b48f058d06d395010b6cdfc7744b49de671d76bbac4ad94ae1 (pam_pkcs11.so)

UDEV Backdoor
7bd8061b8e39ace106e83256c8f01455701014029366ff9030fd65ccb3eb2b75 (apm-events-d)  

== Persistence Mechanisms

/etc/pam.d/sshd
# PKCS#11 smart card authentication support
auth       sufficient   pam_pkcs11.so

/etc/udev/rules.d/99-apm-events.rules
# APM device event monitoring
# Triggers event handler daemon on random device initialisation
ACTION=="add", ENV{MAJOR}=="1", ENV{MINOR}=="8", RUN+="/lib/udev/apm-events-d run"

== Behavioral Analysis

The UDEV malware masquerades as "kworker/u4:2" by overwriting argv[0], then overwrites its own executable before execution.  

The PAM backdoor checks for the hardcoded password: Wr41thK3y_2024. On match, SSH access is granted. On failure, it exfiltrates credentials via DNS using res_query function.  

== Code Artifacts

Both samples employ identical string obfuscation techniques. Decrypted strings recovered:

"WR-2024-ALPHA"
"telemetry-svc.invalid"
"Wr41thK3y_2024"

This discovery underscores the sophistication and diversity of Linux-targeted malware threats.

items.content:
RT @vxunderground: I've praised a few malwares for various reasons. However, this particular malware is very interesting.

- Initially masquerading malware, designed to target very specific audience 

- Written in multiple programming languages. However, the first stage is written in an uncommon programming language (Delphi) and compiled using an uncommon compiler (Embarcadero), specifically Delphi GUI TForm from Embarcadero (Vcl?)

- Obfuscated, in a very natural way. The binary at first glance appears semi-legitimate, it hides itself well

- The first stage (stager, or packer) contains multiple layers of decoy data. It makes reverse engineering challenging, not due to difficulty but time exhaustion

- Secondary stage (where I'm currently at) is loaded into memory discretely, it flows naturally with the GUI application. When decompiled, the stager has over 15,000 functions. It makes finding the in-memory loaded secondary stage tricky

- The secondary stage has some form of interprocess communication, it relies on the first stage to load it. If the first stage is not present, it does not work.

- The second stage works (in a currently unknown capacity) to load a third stage payload. However, the secondary stage with the first stage work (in a currently unknown way) to decrypt the third (and potentially final) stage a/k/a the actual payload

- The second stage uses deterministic probability to alert the first stage if the machine executing the first stage is a virtual machine and/or anti malware environment.

- The second stage has multiple integrity checks, it ensures it has not been tampered with to force the binary to pull the third and final stage.

This malware is pretty tricky. It definitely hasn't been written by a noob. This is definitely a very skilled Threat Actor who is using AI to supercharge their code base. Based on my conversations with my colleague, and information he can share, this code base has been rapidly evolving over the past couple of months in a uncharacteristic manner. While this Threat Actor has always shown evolution and improvement, it is now much faster, precise, and flexible.

Overall, based on what I've seen so far, they've put in a lot of work to make this as painful as possible. In order to successfully reverse engineer this binary, it require outside the box thinking and/or building a custom solution to successfully trick the secondary stager to give up the goop (the third stage)... or a custom extractor to pull the third stage statically.

No solution is ideal. This is good malware. If it's not state-sponsored, it's someone who has been doing this a long time and knows ball.

items.content:
RT @lauriewired: Physical Hardware is often (artificially) softlocked by firmware.

One of the biggest “unlock” hacks in history happened on IBM’s POWER8.

IBM Servers are kinda weird. They often ship with 40+ processor cores installed, but you only get to use whatever was licensed. As a business, you could then “upgrade in place” later, once you had the money.

Well, unless you take advantage of a funny firmware bug.

IBM POWER workloads run on a hypervisor, which divides physical system resources into pools.

Due to a synchronization bug (sort of like a double-spend in finance), if you moved pools around fast enough, you could add resources faster than they were removed!

The author went from 8 -> 40 POWER8 cores. Depending on the server you bought, you could have gone even further, from 8 -> 192 cores!

Probably the biggest unlock (in terms of “allowed” FLOPS to “unlocked” FLOPS) in history!

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: Call stack spoofing started in the game hacking community on UnknownCheats in 2018. A single JMP [RBX] gadget to spoof a return address.

Eight years later it defeats every layer of EDR call-stack-based detection and is CET shadow stack compatible.

The evolution:

@namazso (2018) – original x64 return address spoofing from the game hacking scene. The foundation everything else built on.

@waldoirc YouMayPasser (2022) – first major extension of namazso’s work, bypassing PE-sieve and Moneta using Gargoyle-style ROP with sleep encryption.

@KlezVirus SilentMoonwalk (2022) – desynchronized stack unwinding using real .pdata RUNTIME_FUNCTION entries to construct synthetic frames. Moonwalk++ (2025) combined stack spoofing with memory self-encryption.

@0xmaz LACUNA Chain (2026) – Ghost Frames defeating userland hooks, kernel callbacks, and ETW-Ti stack collection simultaneously. Zero .pdata modification.

BingusLdr (2026) – CET compatible stack spoofing. The shadow stack problem every previous technique ignored, solved.

Commercial C2 frameworks like Havoc Pro from @infinitycurve have already started integrating CET compatible stack spoofing to bypass top tier EDRs. But vendors like @elasticseclabs are catching on, publishing research on detecting shadow stack mismatches and synthetic frame anomalies.

The arms race continues. From game cheats to defeating enterprise EDRs. The tradecraft is the same. The targets changed.

If you build detections for call stack anomalies, this is the history you need to understand.
